zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription follows the supplied BnF scan; lexical data do not determine damaged glyphs.

lines.note: Sǒsǒ is glossed by Fajimurugui, beginning an action. The medial letter is short s rather than the provisional e, and Portuguese fazer begins with f; the visible spacing separates começar a fazer.

This separate Sǒſô concerns burial, explained by the Japanese forms for burying and sending off. The second vowel mark is worn beside the long ſ; enlarged reinspection favors a circumflex, with the following Sǒsôſuru providing a local comparison. The first vowel has a caron, and Vt introduces the example below.
Sǒsôſuru means to bury. Its short medial s and the following long ſ are distinct printed forms, retained within this indented example.
Sosǒ describes something roughly made, with Araqi catachi identifying a coarse form. The damaged but visible initial S is restored; groſ- begins the Portuguese adjective continued below.
Seira completes grosseira, followed by tosca, 'rough' or 'crude.' This short row remains a continuation of the Sosǒ entry.
Soſo is explained in Latin as the female genitals. The e of mulieris is weak in the scan; the connected Latin word is chosen rather than treating the provisional gap as a separate word.
Soſocǒxij describes an inattentive or flustered person. The Portuguese continues the description with restlessness on the next row.

The body phrase describes the person as restless; the scan reads in quieta, not inguteta. At the far right, (Depreßa. is the displaced gloss for the following adverb entry, retained on this physical row in separate right-hand parts.

Sǒſocu and Saſſocu express promptness, further explained by Fayacu ſumiyaca. The alternative-form marker is l, not i, and the headword ends cu rather than tu. Its Portuguese gloss Depreßa is displaced to the right of the preceding row.
The adjective Sǒſocuna describes something hurried. The first vowel's visible mark is restored; the Portuguese retains the printed apreßada ligature.
The corresponding adverb means hurriedly. Aduer. is an abbreviated grammatical label, and the first vowel's mark agrees with the adjacent adjectival entry.
Soſocuracaxi is followed by the preferred form Soſoyacaxi, introduced by Potiùs. The conjugational information runs through ſu into caita on the next row.

runs.text: Prouocar, ou irritar a alguem a que ſe

lines.note: Caita completes the conjugation listed above. The Portuguese defines provoking or irritating someone into becoming angry or quarrelling.

runs.text: agaſte, ou brigue com outro, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the sense of provoking a quarrel. Iy ſo- starts an example in which speech incites the other person; the compound is physically continued below.
Soſocuracaſu completes Iy ſo-ſocuracaſu. Idem ties this example to the immediately preceding sense of verbal provocation.
Soſomeqi means speaking softly or confidentially. The Portuguese has à puri-, without the provisional extra e, and the final hyphen divides puridade across rows.
Dade completes puridade, a private or whispered manner of speaking. Saſayaqu is the Japanese equivalent introduced by ideſt.

runs.text: Couſa malfeita, ou großeira, ou toſ-

lines.note: Soſǒna describes something badly made, coarse or rough. The worn first o is retained as a vowel rather than punctuation, and malfeita restores the visible t omitted by the provisional reading.

runs.text: ca. Item, Peßoa deſatentada, & que faz as

lines.note: Ca completes tosca. Item adds the sense of an inattentive person whose actions are badly executed, developed on the following row.
The person does things badly and imperfectly. Imperfeita has f, not long ſ; the historical separate mente is retained rather than modernized to one word.
Sosǒni is the adverb corresponding to the preceding rough or careless adjective. The scan's damaged vowels and short medial s yield this reading, replacing the malformed provisional Sagoni.
Soſoqi means pouring or scattering water. The Portuguese object begins a-goa across this row break and is completed below.

runs.text: goa come com a mão, Iſopo, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Describes sprinkling water with the hand or an aspergillum. The scan appears to print come com; that awkward wording is retained, not silently changed to como com. Miz- starts the example's Japanese object.
Zu follows Miz- to form Mizzuuo ſoſoqu, sprinkling water. Ame ſoſoqu introduces the rain-related example glossed on the next row; P. is printed upright as a usage label.
Chouiſcar means to drizzle and is the gloss of Ame ſoſoqu above. It remains an indented continuation, not a separate Portuguese heading.
Soſori means choosing or taking out things for sorting. The conjugational forms ſoru and ſotta belong to this verb; cou- begins cousas across the row break.

runs.text: ſas da meſma laya, & apartalas como Cha, me-

lines.note: The objects are of the same kind and are separated, such as tea or medicines. Cha occurs inside the Portuguese explanation; me- begins the next example noun.
Zinhas completes mezinhas, medicines. Soſorinoquru introduces selecting and discarding material; Eſco- begins the Portuguese verbal explanation continued below.
Completes escolhendo botar fora, throwing something out in the course of sorting. The short row closes the preceding compound-verb example.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de Cha, que fica entre meo,

lines.note: This nominal Soſori is an intermediate grade of tea. Hũa and entre meo retain the original nasal abbreviation and historical expression.

runs.text: de pois de ſe tirar o milhor, & ficar o ſomenos.

lines.note: The tea remains after the best portion has been removed, with the inferior portion left behind. The printed de pois and milhor are retained rather than modernized.
Soſoridaxi means selecting and cleaning tea or similar material. Its conjugation ſu, daita is retained as printed, with the object continued below.
Cha, &c. completes the object of selecting and cleaning. The row belongs to Soſoridaxi rather than a new tea entry.

runs.text: Oßos, & penas que os falcões vo-

lines.note: Soſoro denotes the bones and feathers regurgitated by hawks. The last vo- begins vomitão across the physical line boundary; Oßos retains the printed ligature.

runs.text: mitão fora depois de comer algum paßaro.

lines.note: Completes the statement that hawks vomit these remains after eating a bird. The scan's fora begins with f, not the provisional long ſ.
Soſorouo vtçu means to cast or regurgitate these remains. The paragraph mark introduces an example within the same falconry entry.

Soſoyacaxi, without the provisional extra i, refers back to Soſocuracaxi. Enlarged comparison with the clear Vide in c2-l045 shows that this line actually prints anomalous Tide, which is retained. The printed space in Soſo curacaxi and abbreviated u also remain unregularized.
Soſoyaqi, alternatively Saſayaqu, means speaking privately or whispering. The alternative marker l and the Japanese forms remain roman, while the Portuguese gloss is italic.

runs.text: Voz baixa como de quem fala

lines.note: Soſoyaqigoye denotes a low voice such as that of someone speaking confidentially. Goye is part of the compound headword, not a separate embedded term.
À puridade completes the description of the low, confidential voice. The grave accent and the continuation placement are retained.

runs.text: Pouco a pouco. Item, hum pouco.

lines.note: Soſſoto means little by little and also a little. The doubled long ſ is retained rather than normalizing the heading to a different contemporary spelling.
Sôtai is the entire body, explicitly paraphrased as Subeteno tai. The Portuguese noun is corpo, not the provisional corço.
A separate Sǒtai entry means green moss and is glossed by Auoi coqe. The spelling Auoi is retained rather than modernizing the Japanese adjective.
Sôtaixǒ means a commander-in-chief or general. The distinct circumflex and caron signs in the headword are retained as printed.

Sotan, alternatively ſǒten, refers to early morning. Fayaqi axita explains the time of day, and the historical Polamenhãa is retained. Enlarged reinspection does not establish a vowel mark over the first heading’s o, so no accent is imported from the lexical index.
Cedo, ou de madrugada completes the early-morning definition. This is a continuation of Sotan, not a separate adverb entry.

Sôtat here means addressing the king, explained by Sôxi taſuru. The scan supports the terminal t in the headword, ao rather than o, and the worn e in Rey; it is not the malformed provisional Sotaxt or Ry.
A separate Sôtat means running. The scan prints Vaxiri with V, an anomalous form not silently changed to expected Faxiri, and visibly doubles the long ſ in taſſuru. The usage label S. is upright.
Sǒtçǔ means agreeing or being in accord, explained by Ai tçǔzuru. Pa- begins parecer, opinion, across the physical row break.
Recer completes agreeing in opinion and will with someone. Goin begins a musical example continued on the following row; this is an indented continuation, not a new heading.

The lower-case ſǒtçǔ completes Goin ſǒtçǔ, the agreement of five musical tones. The provisional paragraph mark and capital T were spurious; cin- begins cinco below, and the whole row is a continuation.

runs.text: co tõs, ou toadas, que hà na muſica de Iapão.

lines.note: Co completes cinco. The passage refers to five tones or melodies in Japanese music; the printed nasal abbreviation is tõs, restoring the omitted tilde without expanding the word.
Sôtçugǒ is a total or aggregate, explained as Subete auaſuru, combining everything. The Portuguese definition continues with the accounts being summed.

runs.text: contas, ou em ſumma, & aſomando tudo.

lines.note: The definition means the sum of many accounts, or everything added together. The historical aſomando spelling is retained rather than modernized.
Sotdo, alternatively ſotto, denotes the whole earth. The unusual consonant group in Sotdo is printed and is not regularized merely because the alternative form is simpler.
Sǒtei is a grassy courtyard, literally Cuſano niua. The headword has tei, not the provisional tci; the historical Portuguese Pateo is retained.
This Sôtei concerns animal claws or hooves, explained by Tçume and fizzume. The Portuguese noun begins animal, not enimal.
A different Sǒtei is a roughly thatched house, glossed by Cuſano vtena. The definition continues its description of rough construction on the next row.
Completes the rough-construction sense, then adds a poor or lowly house. The scan supports pobre rather than the provisional oobre.
This house-description is used modestly and humbly, qualifying the preceding sense. Falando and humilde replace malformed provisional readings; the separate mente is retained.
Sǒten means early in the morning, explained by Axita tocu. The initial i is the explanatory marker, unlike the alternative-form l elsewhere.
Another Sǒten refers to the blue-looking sky. Auoqi ſora supplies the Japanese explanation, and q̃ is preserved as the printed Portuguese abbreviation.

runs.text: Hũas aruores que ha nas niuas de Ia-

lines.note: Sotet denotes trees in Japanese gardens, likened to palms below. The medial letter is t, not c. Enlargement shows staining above the o rather than a secure circumflex, so the headword is read unaccented. Niuas is the Japanese garden term embedded in Portuguese; Ia- continues Iapão.
Pão completes Iapão. The trees resemble palms; the weak middle of palmeiras is read as m rather than the provisional separated v, without claiming the trees are botanically true palms.
Sotji denotes inattention or lack of consideration. The scan has t rather than c in the heading, and Item opens an additional sense continued below.
Adds that Sotji sometimes denotes insufficient courtesy or reverence. Aliquãdo is retained with its printed nasal abbreviation.
Sotjina, alternatively ſotjino, describes something inattentive or discourteous. The Portuguese adjective deſcortes is displaced to the far right of the following physical row.

Sotjini is the adverbial counterpart of Sotjina. Enlarged reinspection shows no secure caron on the first vowel; the provisional accent is removed. At the far right, (deſcortes. completes the preceding adjective's definition rather than this grammatical label.
Sǒtǒ means fitting or being suitable, explained by Aiataru. Both headword vowels carry visible marks; conueniente replaces the provisional conuemiente, and qua- begins quadrar.
Drar completes quadrar, to fit. Sǒtǒ xita coto illustrates a suitable thing, whose Portuguese adjective continues over the next row break.
Niente completes conueniente and closes the example. This fragment is not a separate lexical entry.
Soto, alternatively ſotto, is an adverb meaning a little. It is distinct from the following equine-anatomy term despite their similar spellings.

runs.text: Ilharga, ou vazio da barriga do caualo

lines.note: Sôtô denotes the flank or hollow of a horse's belly. The two circumflex marks are retained, and the location is further specified on the next row.

runs.text: junto dos pees dos quartos dianteiros.

lines.note: Locates the hollow near the feet of the forequarters. Enlarged reinspection establishes two e-types in the historical pees, restoring the second e omitted in the provisional text; no modern accent or spelling is substituted.
Soto means outside, with Foca as the Japanese explanation. Sotoye izzu- begins the example 'go outside,' physically continued below.
Ru completes izzuru, to go out. Sair pera fora is the full Portuguese gloss, retaining the historical preposition pera.
Sôto is glossed simply as Bonzos, Buddhist clerics. The heading's long-vowel mark distinguishes it graphically from the adjacent Soto entries.

runs.text: Pao agudo na ponta que poem na ca-

lines.note: Sotoba is a pointed wooden grave marker. Ca- begins cabeceira, locating it at the head of the grave in the following row.

runs.text: beceira das ſepulturas, em que eſcreuem algum

lines.note: Beceira completes cabeceira. The passage explains that an inscription is written on the grave marker; the sentence continues with its possible forms below.
The writing is an inscription or epitaph. Sotobauo tatçu- begins the example for erecting these markers; the scan supports a cedilla in tatçu, omitted by the provisional reading.
Ru completes tatçuru. The Portuguese describes erecting these wooden markers at graves, closing the example begun above.

Sôtǒjǔ names a sect, additionally designated Yeguesô. The embedded Portuguese expression refers to Ienxǔs; the vowel and its visible caron replace the malformed Ienxis, without importing the different accent used on another page.

runs.text: Hũ pouco pera cada hũ. Vt,

lines.note: Sottozzutçu means a little for each person. Both hũ abbreviations remain unexpanded, and Vt introduces the following distribution example.
Sottozzutçu vaquru means distributing a little to each person. The Portuguese sentence continues with the portion allotted to each below.
Seu pouco completes each person's small share. The short indented row closes the distribution example rather than beginning another entry.

So v is irregular rain, explained by Voroſocana ame. The headword has a visible space between So and v. Chuua restores the vowel omitted by the provisional Chua, retaining the printed u-type; deſ- continues desordenada below.
Completes desordenada and explains that the rain is sometimes hard, sometimes gentle. The contrast belongs to the single rain entry above.
Soua is a mountain flank. Souazzutaiuo begins an example of following that flank, with ſuru on the next physical row.

runs.text: Ir ao longo, ou polla ilharga do mon-

lines.note: Suru completes Souazzutaiuo ſuru, travelling along a mountainside. The Portuguese reads Ir ao as separate words; mon- starts monte across the row break.

runs.text: te por lugares perigoſos, ou eſtreitos.

lines.note: Te completes monte. The route passes through dangerous or narrow places; the scan's tall long ſ in eſtreitos is retained rather than the provisional short s.
Souari means increasing or being added. The Portuguese infinitive Acrecentarſe includes the r omitted in the provisional reading; ajũtarſe retains its nasal abbreviation.
Souazzutai refers the reader back to Soua and its mountainside-travel example. Vide is the italic cross-reference label, not part of the Japanese heading.

Sǒuô expresses proportion or suitability, explained by Ai vôzuru. Enlargement reveals the faint caron over the first o as well as the final circumflex. The Portuguese nasal abbreviations in cõueniẽcia remain unexpanded.

Sǒuôna describes a proportionate or suitable thing. The headword begins S and contains u, not the provisional Bǒnôna. Enlarged comparison shows conueniẽte, with a full n after o and a nasal abbreviation only over the later e, rather than cimueniete.
